title: Hot Cocoa Mix

drivers.name: price increase (no promotion)
drivers.evidence: Price increased to $5.03 (+3.1%) from $4.88. Past promotions at lower prices lifted sales x1.04 on average (noise-adjusted). No discount this week. Price increase likely reduces demand; prior non-promo weeks at $5.03 show low sales (23, 26).

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 34.0. The target week has no event but a price increase to $5.03 (+3.1% vs regular $4.88), which is above recent promotion prices. Past promotions (11 total) show a median lift of x1.18, noise-adjusted x1.04, but the current price is not discounted—so no uplift. The week after a promotion typically sees x0.78 (noise-adjusted), but the last promotion was 4 weeks ago (2026-04-20), so no carryover effect. The Mother's Day week before (2025-04-28) showed x0.86, but noise-adjusted x1.0. No other drivers. The classical model suggests x0.78, but that’s driven by a past post-promo dip not applicable here. Price increase likely suppresses demand. Evidence is thin but consistent: no promotion, no event, price up. Adjust down modestly.

PRODUCT: Hot Cocoa Mix | category Grocery | Store #12 (Austin, TX)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 5.03 (+3.1% vs regular price 4.88)

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 34.0 | 5%-95%: 15.8 - 47.4 | 10%-90%: 20.6 - 46.4

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-45% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
